title: Stephan's Quintet

author: Sofia Rossi

body.text: Trustless networks live or die by the cryptographic guarantees behind Stephan's Quintet. Here is how the underlying protocol design solves coordination and verification without central intermediaries.

Stephan's Quintet is a visual grouping of five galaxies in the constellation Pegasus, four of which form a physical associated compact group designated Hickson Compact Group 92. It was the first compact galaxy group to be discovered and one of the most well studied systems of its kind.

The group was discovered by Édouard Stephan in 1877 using the 80 cm reflector telescope at the Marseille Observatory. The brightest member of the apparent grouping is NGC 7320, while the brightest member of the physical association is NGC 7318B.

Radio observations in the late 1970s revealed a filament of emission between the galaxies in the group. Observations with modern space telescopes identified the filament as a shock wave, caused by the high-speed intruder (NGC 7318B) colliding with the intragroup medium (IGrM) at approximately 850, 1,000 kilometers per second.

Stephan's Quintet contains at least 13 candidate tidal dwarf galaxies, with several located in the tidal tail connecting to NGC 7319. A nearby galaxy, NGC 7320C, has been proposed as an earlier intruder responsible for the formation of the inner and outer tidal tails of NGC 7319.

High-sensitivity observations by the FAST and MeerKAT revealed a massive diffuse reservoir of neutral hydrogen (H I) surrounding the group, indicating that its galaxies have undergone substantial gas stripping.
NGC 7319 hosts the only confirmed active galactic nucleus in Stephan's Quintet, while NGC 7317 and NGC 7320 may also host AGNs, but their presence remains unconfirmed.

Stephan's Quintet was selected as one of the five cosmic objects observed by the James Webb Space Telescope as part of the release of its first official science images. Observations of the field have enabled studies of distant background galaxies, allowing astronomers to investigate galaxy evolution in the early universe.
It has been featured several times on Astronomy Picture of the Day.

Environment

In 1973, astronomer Halton Arp conducted a radio survey of the surrounding field of Stephan's Quintet using the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's 210-foot telescope. The survey identified NGC 7331, Anon and NGC 7363.

Earlier observations suggested NGC 7331 and NGC 7320 were connected by a faint radio bridge but subsequent 100, m radio surveys found no evidence of such a structure.
Observations using the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) suggested that the faint filaments in the field of Stephan's Quintet might be Galactic cirrus, diffuse dust structures in the Milky Way.
Radio detections detected a detached magnetized cloud located in the foreground void space between the Milky Way and Stephan's Quintet, with a rotation measure of approximately +240 rad m−2.
Local environment

The field surrounding Stephan's Quintet contains 21 galaxies, comprising four ellipticals, one lenticular and 16 spirals. Stephan's Quintet is located in a relatively low galaxy surface density environment, but it contains an unusually high number of elliptical early-type galaxies.
Several HI-emitting galaxies were detected in the surrounding field of Stephan's Quintet, known as Anon 1 through 9.

In the catalog's terminology, an "open" galaxy cluster lacks a pronounced concentration of galaxies, while a "near" cluster belongs to a distance class defined by a recession velocity below 15,000 km/s.

The redshift of the brightest member of Stephan's Quintet, NGC 7318, places Stephan's Quintet within the Perseus, Pisces Supercluster.

Deep field observations

The field surrounding Stephan's Quintet was chosen as a "public field" for JWST's Early Release Observations (ERO), making its JWST observations immediately available to the community. JWST observations have been used to search for quiescent galaxies in the early universe (z = 2, 5).
Interactions and dynamical history
Earlier Interactions

NGC 7320C, known as the "first collider" or "old intruder", is proposed to have undergone several encounters with NGC 7319 approximately 500 million years ago and produced parallel tidal tails known as the "young" tail and "old" tail.

The "young" tail extends for more than 100 kiloparsecs (kpc), while the "old" tail is the oldest identified tidal structure in Stephan's Quintet, is approximately 100 kpc long and is connected to the shock zones by a compact H I cloud.
The interaction of NGC 7320C and NGC 7319 contributed a significant mass of stripped stars to the common halo of the group.

H I observations with MeerKAT associated with NGC 7320C provide further information about its proposed interaction with NGC 7319. H I observations revealed approximately 2×108 M⊙ of atomic gas, distributed across approximately 20 kpc. Studies found no detectable H I connection between NGC 7320C and tidal tails of Stephan's Quintet.
Because NGC 7320C has a redshift and low relative velocity similar to NGC 7319, astronomers suggest that NGC 7320C made a relatively slow passage.
Collision involving NGC 7318B

ROSAT's High Resolution Imager (HRI) revealed an elongated structure in the intragroup medium (IGrM) between NGC 7319 and NGC 7318B. This structure appears sharply bounded, extends approximately 40 kpc and was identified as a shock front.

This structure is thought to have formed when NGC 7318B collided with the stripped gas of Stephan's Quintet at approximately 850, 1000 km/s. Astronomers consider the collision to be at an early stage because NGC 7318B still retains most of its neutral hydrogen (H I) gas and several H II regions.

IGrM is filled with hot, low-density gas, which exist between the spaces of galaxies in a galaxy group. Shock front is a boundary where the physical conditions undergo an abrupt change because of a shock wave.
Shock fronts heat the gas and produce discontinuities in temperature and density, which are mainly observed in the X-ray wavelength.

By analyzing the spectral aging of relativistic electrons, astronomers determined that the high-speed collision began at the northern end of the shock ridge approximately 20 million years ago and propagated southward, finishing its impact ~5-6 million years ago.

The geometry of the collision suggests that the intruder galaxy NGC 7318B struck the tidal filaments at a shallow angle of approximately 15°. The collision is inferred to occur at an angle of approximately 58° relative to the line of sight. 6 keV rather than the approximately 2 keV predicted from a head-on collision.

The radio data also exclude the possibility of weak shocks (M ≈ 2, 4) propagating through the hot X-ray gas, as the weak shocks are unable to produce the flat spectral indices and their expected radio luminosity is low.

Astronomers suggest that the shock must be driven directly into the cold, dense H I gas, producing a shock with a high-Mach-number (Mach 40, 100). Astronomers also suggest that adiabatic compression of a preexisting electron population is implausible, as no seeds (fossil electrons) have been observed and the Mach numbers conflict with the X-ray observations.
Numerical Simulations
Collisionless N-body simulations suggested that a single encounter by a companion galaxy was less likely to account for the formation of both "inner" and "outer" tidal tails of NGC 7319.
